title: Is Blue Moon Woke? | VirtueVigil Review

wokeInstances.name: Normalization of Non-Traditional Sexuality
wokeInstances.description: Hart's homosexuality/bisexuality is the emotional core. He declares himself 'omnisexual,' flirts with a delivery boy, and his closeted existence is presented as a source of suffering. Organic because Hart was historically gay.

wokeInstances.name: The Sympathetic Outsider
wokeInstances.description: Hart framed as brilliant outsider — Jewish, gay, short, alcoholic — whose marginalization is society's loss. Historically authentic.

wokeInstances.name: Institutional Evil (implied)
wokeInstances.description: Mid-century America's treatment of gay men as systematically cruel, depicted through implication and internalized oppression rather than direct institutional confrontation.

traditionalInstances.name: Consequences of Vice
traditionalInstances.description: Hart's alcoholism destroys everything — career, partnership, love, life. No redemption arc. He dies from it seven months later. Vice has consequences, period.

traditionalInstances.name: Personal Accountability
traditionalInstances.description: Hart is not presented as a victim. He sabotaged his own career through self-pity and alcoholism. The film holds him accountable even while acknowledging the constraints of his era.

traditionalInstances.name: Industry & Perseverance / Artistic Discipline
traditionalInstances.description: Hart's lament for craftsmanship and sophistication is inherently conservative. He values tradition and the old standards. The film treats this position with respect.

traditionalInstances.name: Wise Elder / Respect for Legacy
traditionalInstances.description: Reverence for Broadway's golden age, the Rodgers and Hart songbook, and artistic tradition. Historical cameos (E. B. White, Sondheim, George Roy Hill) create a tapestry of cultural heritage.

parentalGuidance.sexual: Mild (thematic discussion of sexuality, no nudity)
parentalGuidance.substance: Heavy thematic presence (alcoholism central to story)
